tm-general-form:
The general transfer matrix.

A general form collapses every crossing type into a single two-parameter family. The three nuclear crossings and the connected-sum case become special points of one matrix. Every transfer matrix has the same 2 \times 2 structure, parameterized by two crossing coefficients (c, d):

  T(c, d) = \begin{pmatrix} c(q - q^{-1}) + d & c \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}

The coefficients (c, d) \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1/2}] depend on how the two knots interact. For knots meeting via connected sum, the Jones polynomial satisfies J_{K_1 \# K_2} = J_{K_1} \cdot J_{K_2}, giving c = 1 and d = 0. For knots meeting via the Hecke product (the physically relevant case for nucleon crossings), the coefficients are determined by the representation-theoretic structure of the crossing. They do not reduce to connected-sum formulas. The three nuclear crossing types have specific (c, d) values listed in Section 3.2.

The transfer matrix acts on a Iwahori--Hecke algebra element a\sigma_i + b by left multiplication and Hecke reduction (T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1):

  \begin{pmatrix} a' \\ b' \end{pmatrix} = T(c, d) \cdot \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}

Explicitly:

  a' = ac(q - q^{-1}) + ad + bc, \qquad b' = ac + bd

Three properties fix how the crossing acts: its determinant controls invertibility, its eigenvalues control spectral behavior under iteration, and its degenerate limits recover the connected-sum and scalar matrices.

Determinant. The determinant governs whether the crossing action is invertible:

  \det T(c, d) = cd(q - q^{-1}) + d^2 - c^2

Eigenvalues (when c \neq 0). The eigenvalues give the spectral behavior of the crossing under repeated application:

  \lambda_{\pm} = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[c(q - q^{-1}) + 2d \pm \sqrt{\bigl[c(q - q^{-1})\bigr]^2 + 4c^2}\Bigr]

Special cases. The two degenerations of interest recover matrices met earlier: c = 0 collapses T to the scalar matrix, while c = 1, d = 0 gives the connected-sum (fundamental) matrix.

  • c = 0: T(0, d) = d \cdot \mathbb{I} (scalar matrix)
  • d = 0: T(c, 0) = c \cdot \begin{pmatrix} q - q^{-1} & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
  • c = 1, d = 0: The fundamental matrix T_{pp}
sec:tm-knot-pairs-intro:
Every interaction in this framework is a crossing between two knotted strands. The knot polynomial that records such a crossing is an unbounded object whose degree grows with knot complexity. A transfer matrix trades this unbounded data for a fixed-size operator: to each pair of knots one assigns a 2 \times 2 matrix over \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1/2}]. This compresses the polynomial content into four Laurent-polynomial entries obtained from the Hecke reduction. The payoff is composition: because every crossing carries a matrix of the same shape, a chain of crossings becomes a matrix product, and interactions of very different physical character can be iterated on equal footing.

The smallest case makes the compression visible. Two unknotted strands (the vacuum--vacuum pair) carry no knotting at all, yet their crossing does not reduce to the identity. The Hecke relation still fires, producing the simplest non-identity transfer matrix. That a genuinely empty configuration produces a non-trivial matrix indicates the transfer matrix records the crossing itself, not merely the knots.

This section builds the catalogue crossing type by crossing type. It begins with the trivial matrices, passes to the nuclear matrices, then to the electromagnetic matrices, and closes by sorting the entire list into a short classification.
tm-knot-pairs:
Transfer matrices of knot pairs.

A transfer matrix records how a single crossing between two knotted strands acts on the Hecke chain. Each knot pair contributes a 2 \times 2 block determined by its crossing coefficients c and d. Every nuclear and electromagnetic crossing reduces to one of just three classes (Section 5). This section lists every transfer matrix for each knot pair over \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1/2}].

1. Trivial transfer matrices

1a. Unknot--unknot (vacuum--vacuum) Knots: K_1 = T_{1,0}, K_2 = T_{1,0}. Jones polynomials: J_{T_{1,0}}(q) = 1, J_{T_{1,0} \# T_{1,0}}(q) = 1. Crossing coefficients: c = 1, d = 0.

  T_{\nu\nu}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} q - q^{-1} & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

This is the simplest non-identity transfer matrix.

1b. Identity (no crossing) When two strands do not cross at generator \sigma_i, the transfer matrix is the identity:

  T_{\varnothing}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbb{I}

This is the c = 0, d = 1 case.

2. Nuclear transfer matrices (proton--neutron pairs)

These three matrices govern all nuclear interactions.

2a. Proton--proton (\mathfrak{p}-\mathfrak{p}) Strands: two up quarks, each an unknot strand of \mathcal{B}_3 with positive crossing orientation (lepton partner T_{2,3}). Crossing coefficients: c = 1, d = 0.

  T_{pp}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} q - q^{-1} & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

Explicit entries are in Table 1. Eigenvalues are \lambda_{\pm} = \frac{1}{2}\left((q - q^{-1}) \pm \sqrt{(q-q^{-1})^2 + 4}\right).

2b. Neutron--neutron (\mathfrak{n}-\mathfrak{n}) Strands: two down quarks, each an unknot strand of \mathcal{B}_3 with negative crossing orientation (lepton partner T_{2,3}^{\sigma}). Crossing coefficients: c = 1, d = -(q - q^{-1}).

  T_{nn}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -(q - q^{-1}) \end{pmatrix}

Explicit entries are in Table 2. Relation to T_{pp}: T_{nn}(q) = T_{pp}(q) - (q - q^{-1}) \mathbb{I}.

2c. Mixed (\mathfrak{p}-\mathfrak{n}) Strands: one up and one down quark, unknot strands of opposite crossing orientation (lepton partners T_{2,3} and T_{2,3}^{\sigma}). Crossing coefficients: c = 1, d = -\frac{1}{2}(q - q^{-1}).

  T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} & 1 \\ 1 & -\frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} \end{pmatrix}

Explicit entries are in Table 3. Midpoint property: T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q) = \frac{1}{2}(T_{pp}(q) + T_{nn}(q)). This gives beta decay a universal matrix.

3. Electromagnetic transfer matrices

3a. Photon--electron (\gamma-e) Motifs: chiral photon superposition 1 + \phi_0\sigma_0 + \phi_1\sigma_1 + \phi_{01}\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1} (bare identity sector K_1 = \varnothing), electron e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 \in B_3 closing to the positive Hopf link T(2,2) (single-component alternative T_{2,3}). On the inter-strand crossing channel (c = 1, d = 0):

  T_{\gamma e}(q) = T_{pp}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} q - q^{-1} & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

The bare photon identity channel contributes no crossing deformation.

3b. Electron--electron (e-e) Motifs: two electrons e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 \in B_3 (Hopf closure T(2,2)) of identical chirality:

  T_{ee}(q) = T_{pp}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} q - q^{-1} & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

3c. Photon--photon (\gamma-\gamma) Bare identity sectors K_1 = \varnothing, K_2 = \varnothing:

  T_{\gamma\gamma}(q) = T_{\nu\nu}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} q - q^{-1} & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

3d. Photon--positron (\gamma-e^+) Bare photon sector K_1 = \varnothing paired with positron e^+ = \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1} \in B_3 (mirror Hopf closure):

  T_{\gamma e^+}(q) = T_{pp}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} q - q^{-1} & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

3e. Electron--positron (e^--e^+) Opposite-chirality pair e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 and e^+ = \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1}:

  T_{e^-e^+}(q) = T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} & 1 \\ 1 & -\frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} \end{pmatrix}

4. Higher-generation transfer matrices

4a. Unknot--trefoil (general: any partner with unknot) For any knot K paired with the unknot T_{1,0}, the connected sum gives c = 1. In the nuclear context, the unknot contributes c = 1, d = 0. Therefore T_{T_{1,0}, K}(q) = T_{pp}(q) for every knot K. The unknot is universally invisible. The same applies to the photon.

4b. Cinquefoil--cinquefoil (\mathfrak{b}-\mathfrak{b}) Knots: K_1 = T_{2,5}, K_2 = T_{2,5} (lepton partners; the quarks are unknot strands). c = 1, d = 0. Thus T_{\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{b}}(q) = T_{pp}(q). All same-chirality identical-knot pairs give T_{pp}.

4c. Trefoil--cinquefoil (\mathfrak{u}-\mathfrak{b}) Knots: K_1 = T_{2,3}, K_2 = T_{2,5} (lepton partners; the quarks are unknot strands). c = 1, d = 0. Thus T_{\mathfrak{u}\mathfrak{b}}(q) = T_{pp}(q).

4d. T_{3,4}--T_{3,4} (Hopf{}^2--Hopf{}^2, color binding) Knots: K_1 = T_{3,4}, K_2 = T_{3,4}. c = 1, d = 0. Thus T_{\mathfrak{t}\mathfrak{t}}(q) = T_{pp}(q).

4e. Knot--mirror knot (any K with K^{\sigma}) Via connected sum, T_{K,K^{\sigma}} = T_{pp}. But for nucleon crossings (via Hecke product), non-trivial coefficients arise. This distinguishes T_{nn} and T_{\mathrm{mix}}.

5. Summary: classification of all transfer matrices

Every transfer matrix falls into one of three classes. See Table 4. The identity matrix \mathbb{I} is the degenerate c = 0, d = 1 case. Key identities: T_{\mathrm{mix}} = \frac{1}{2}(T_{pp} + T_{nn}), T_{nn} = T_{pp} - (q - q^{-1}) \mathbb{I}, and T_{\gamma e} = T_{ee} = T_{\gamma\gamma} = T_{\nu\nu} = T_{\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{b}} = T_{\mathfrak{t}\mathfrak{t}} = T_{pp}.

sec:tm-interactions-intro:
A transfer matrix records a single configuration of interacting braid strands; an interaction is a change from one such configuration to another. Since every crossing type carries a transfer matrix, the change an interaction induces is simply the difference between the matrix after the interaction and the matrix before it. This encodes disparate processes—beta decay, photon absorption, pair creation—as a single operator on a 2 \times 2 matrix, so they can be compared and iterated.

Converting one neutron into a proton advances a nuclear crossing type by one step—from T_{nn} to T_{\mathrm{mix}}—and the change is the difference \Delta = T_{\mathrm{after}} - T_{\mathrm{before}}. Writing this difference as an operator makes the interaction itself the object of study. This section builds the catalogue of such operators.
tm-interactions:
Interaction and decay matrices.

This appendix collects the transfer-matrix changes induced by elementary processes. An interaction changing the crossing type from (K_1, K_2) to (K_1', K_2') is encoded by the \Delta operator:

  \Delta_{K_1 K_2 \to K_1' K_2'}(q) = T_{K_1', K_2'}(q) - T_{K_1, K_2}(q)

1. The universal beta decay matrix

The step from any nuclear crossing type to the next is always the same matrix:

  \Delta_\beta(q) = T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q) - T_{nn}(q) = T_{pp}(q) - T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q) = \tfrac{1}{2}(q - q^{-1}) \mathbb{I}

In explicit entries:

  \Delta_\beta(q) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} \end{pmatrix}

See Table 1. \Delta_\beta is scalar, so it commutes with every transfer matrix. At q = 1, \Delta_\beta = 0 (no classical parity violation). It is universally applicable to every nucleus and converting nucleon.

2. Reverse beta decay (\beta^+)

Positron emission runs \beta^- backwards, undoing the crossing-type change. Its transfer-matrix difference is the negated operator:

  \Delta_{\beta^+}(q) = -\Delta_\beta(q)

3. Photon absorption (Reidemeister I move)

Photon absorption appends a new transfer matrix factor T_{\gamma e} to the chain at the absorbing generator:

  M_i^{(n+1)}(q) = T_{\gamma e}(q) \cdot M_i^{(n)}(q) = T_{pp}(q) \cdot M_i^{(n)}(q)

The energy change for shell n \to n+1 is \Delta E_{n \to n+1} = \hat{V}(M_i^{(n+1)}) - \hat{V}(M_i^{(n)}). For hydrogen, the transfer matrix at shell n is T_{pp}^n, and the energy scales as \lambda_+^n.

4. Pair creation (\gamma\gamma \to e^- e^+)

Pair creation is a chirality-changing crossing replacement of the same form as \beta^+. Its transfer-matrix difference is:

  \Delta_{\mathrm{pair}}(q) = T_{e^- e^+}(q) - T_{\gamma\gamma}(q) = T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q) - T_{pp}(q) = -\Delta_\beta(q)

It consumes a two-photon crossing and produces a particle–antiparticle crossing. A single photon cannot pair-produce in vacuum. The matrix change equals \beta^+ decay.

5. Double beta decay (2\beta)

At a generator \sigma_i affected by converting nucleons at positions p_1 and p_2:

  \Delta M_i^{(2\beta)} = L_i \cdot \Delta_\beta \cdot C_i \cdot \Delta_\beta \cdot R_i + L_i \cdot \Delta_\beta \cdot R_i' + L_i' \cdot \Delta_\beta \cdot R_i

where C_i is the product of unchanged transfer matrices between the converting positions, and L_i, R_i are the products to the left and right. The quadratic term is the nuclear matrix element.

6. Toffoli transfer matrix (information-theoretic)

On 3 strands with nucleon types [\mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{n}], the Toffoli gate selects the target strand whose control--control pair has unit crossing coefficient (c = 1). At the Markov trace weight z = q^3/(q^2+1), the target-flip amplitude is

  P_{7,6}(q) = -\frac{(q-1)(q+1)(q^6+q^4+2q^2+1)}{2q(q^2+1)^2}

The full 2 \times 2 Toffoli transfer matrix \mathbf{M}(q) is in Table 2.

Two withdrawn statements. The factorisation P_{\mathrm{flip}} = c_{k_1k_2}(q)\cdot\Phi(q) with the universal \Phi(q) = (q-1)(q^{3/2}+q^{1/2}-1)(q^{3/2}+q+1)/2(q+1)^2 is retired: \Phi is not in the image of the Toffoli construction under any indexing or convention (Toffoli transfer matrix). And \hat V_1 = z does depend on crossing type — the traced volume at \sigma_1 is \hat V_1(k_1,k_2) = z(q)\,c_{k_1k_2} + d_{k_1k_2}, which reduces to z only for the crossings with (c,d) = (1,0).

7. Catalogue of all \Delta operators

See Table 3.

tm-interaction-completeness:
Interaction completeness: the seven \Sigma_4 transfer matrices.

The embeddability bound on \Sigma_4 yields exactly seven transfer-matrix interactions: six non-trivial force operators plus the identity. See Table.

Double beta decay (2\beta) is not a fresh operator: it is the quadratic composite \Delta_\beta \cdot C \cdot \Delta_\beta at two positions (tm-interactions §5). The Toffoli transfer matrix is a gate construction on three strands, not a fresh interaction.

The count of exactly seven interactions follows from three constraints. First, the crossing-type alphabet on \Sigma_4 carries a quark-flavour pair from \{\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}\}^2, giving four crossing types. Second, Reidemeister-I local completeness requires that single-crossing changes factor through \{T_{pp}, T_{pp}^{-1}\} for emission/absorption plus \{\Delta_\beta, -\Delta_\beta\} for flavour-flip, giving four operators. Pair creation/annihilation reuse \pm\Delta_\beta but at a different crossing-pair structure, giving two further operators. Third, the trivial process makes the operator algebra closed under composition.

Total: 1 + 4 + 2 = 7. The catalogue table is exhaustive: any \Sigma_4-admissible single-crossing change reduces to one of these seven.

rem:qvalue-derivation-chain:
Remark Q-value derivation chain: from q to \beta-decay predictions. The \beta^- decay (Z, N) \to (Z+1, N-1) Q-value is predicted strictly from the aether parameter q, using zero fitting parameters. The calculation operates within the 2 \times 2 standard irreducible representation of H_3(q). While the regular representation is 6 \times 6, the traced-volume computation strictly isolates the 2 \times 2 standard block. MAE \approx 4.4\% across six NNDC benchmarks, zero fitting.

The derivation chain is:

  q \xrightarrow{\text{Hecke}}
  \hat{V}_i(q) \xrightarrow{\text{ratio}}
  \log_q \frac{\hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{dau}}}{\hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{par}}}
  \xrightarrow{\kappa_q}
  \mathcal{Q}(q)

The model output of the chain is the ring element \hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{dau}}/\hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{par}} \in \mathbb{Q}(q) for each generator. The logarithm \log_q, the absolute value and the scale \kappa_q in Steps 2 and 3 are the comparison with measured Q-values, applied after evaluation (mass identity, comparison paragraph).

Step 1. The traced volume \hat{V}_i(q) for each generator \sigma_i is exact in \mathbb{Q}(q):

  \hat{V}_i = z \cdot M_i[0,0] + M_i[1,0],
  \qquad
  M_i = \prod_{j > i} T(\mathfrak{w}^+(i,j), \mathfrak{w}^0(i,j))

where z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1) is the Markov parameter and T(c,d) = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} c(q-q^{-1})+d & c \\ c & d \end{smallmatrix}\right) is the transfer matrix.

Step 2. Classify each generator's log-ratio as unbinding (u), rebinding (r), or unchanged (uc), then q-weight:

  \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{raw}}
  = \bigl| q \cdot \Sigma_u + q^{-1} \cdot \Sigma_r + \Sigma_{uc} \bigr|
    \times \kappa_q

where \kappa_q = \ln(q) \times m_e / 3.

Step 3. Apply shell and pairing corrections (all from q):

  \mathcal{Q}
  = \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{raw}}
    \times F_{\mathrm{shell}}(q)
    \times F_{I_{10}}(Z, N; q)
  • F_{\mathrm{shell}} \approx 0.5904 for shell \geq 5: the Rosso–Jones weighted average over the two degree-2 torus knots \tau(2,9) and \tau(3,4), using the canonical inner product on R(H_r(q)) (canonical inner product). The weights are the quantum dimensions d_\lambda(q), forced by Schur orthogonality — no fitting freedom.
  • F_{I_{10}} = (1 - \delta_{\mathrm{pp}}/Z)(1 - \delta_{\mathrm{nn}}/N) for odd-odd \to even-even at shell \geq 5.
tm-inductive-construction:
Inductive construction (A \to A+1).

Given a nucleus with A nucleons and transfer matrix chains \{M_i\}_{i=0}^{A-2}, this describes how adding one nucleon produces the A+1 nucleus. This inductive step is the engine behind every Skein polynomial computation.

The inductive step: A \to A+1

Given nucleus \mathcal{N}(Z, N) with A nucleons ordered [\tau_0, \ldots, \tau_{A-1}] where \tau_k \in \{\mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{n}\}. The braid has generators \sigma_0, \ldots, \sigma_{A-2} with transfer matrix products M_i and traced volumes \hat{V}_i. Add nucleon \tau_A at position A. Result: Nucleus \mathcal{N}' with A+1 nucleons, generators \sigma_0, \ldots, \sigma_{A-1}, and updated products M_i'.

Rule 1: Existing generators gain one crossing. Every existing generator \sigma_i acquires one crossing between nucleon i and nucleon A. The transfer matrix product appends one new factor on the left:

  M_i'(q) = T_{\tau_i, \tau_A}(q) \cdot M_i(q)

where T_{\tau_i, \tau_A} is T_{pp}, T_{nn}, or T_{\mathrm{mix}}.

Rule 2: One new generator is created. A new generator \sigma_{A-1} appears with a single crossing:

  M_{A-1}'(q) = T_{\tau_{A-1}, \tau_A}(q)

Rule 3: Skein polynomial update. The new polynomial factors as:

  P_{\mathcal{N}'}(q) = \left( \prod_{i=0}^{A-2} \hat{V}_i'(q) \right) \cdot \hat{V}_{A-1}'(q)

where \hat{V}_i'(q) = z \cdot (M_i')_{11} + (M_i')_{21}.

Rule 4: Crossing count grows by A. Adding the (A+1)-th nucleon creates A new crossings. The total crossing count goes from \binom{A}{2} to \binom{A+1}{2}.

The recurrence at each generator

At generator \sigma_i, the coefficients (a_i, b_i) in M_i = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} a_i \\ b_i \end{smallmatrix}\bigr) satisfy the transfer matrix recurrence. Starting from (a, b) = (0, 1), each new crossing with nucleon j updates:

  \begin{pmatrix} a' \\ b' \end{pmatrix} = T(c_j, d_j) \cdot \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}

Explicitly: a' = ac_j(q - q^{-1}) + ad_j + bc_j and b' = ac_j + bd_j.

Jet expansion interpretation

The crossing product stratifies into jet orders. Jet order r is the (r+1)-body correlation, present with multiplicity \binom{k_i}{r}. Adding nucleon A increases the chiral degree at every existing generator by 1. Single beta decay is a 1-jet variation. The Q-value sums only over generators \sigma_i with i \leq p, where p is the converting nucleon's position. Unaffected generators cancel exactly.

Gröbner--Shirshov normal form

The inductive construction produces a canonical normal form at every step. By Rules 1 and 2 the crossings at a fixed generator are contiguous in the braid word and the blocks are ordered by increasing generator index, so the nucleus element is a block-ordered product of linear factors c\,\sigma_i + d \in H_A(q).

Shell closure signatures

At doubly-magic configurations (p, p), the normal form exhibits special structure:

  1. Palindromic histogram. The word-length histogram is a palindrome. For p \neq n, it is not.
  2. Dominant term jump. The dominant coefficient jumps discontinuously. The ratio is larger at shell closures.
  3. Shell energy gap. The Hecke reduction energy drops at shell closures and jumps at the next step.

Complexity bound and magic-shell folding

The total number of matrix multiplications to build \bar{\mathcal{N}}(A) without shell-folding is C_{\mathrm{bare}}(A) = \binom{A}{2}.

At a magic configuration m \in \{2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126\}, the shell-closure signatures identify the closed shell as a single Markov-equivalence class. When the next nucleon is added, it interacts with the collective torus-knot operator T_{2, k} instead of k internal nucleons separately. The folded step costs O(1) matrix multiplications. Folding preserves Reidemeister equivalence because the palindromic histogram certifies the closed shell is in the totally-antisymmetric Wedderburn block. The polynomial agrees identically with the unfolded product.
prop:tm-gs-normal-form:
Proposition Hecke-only Gröbner--Shirshov reduction of the nucleus element. Let \mathcal{N}(Z, N) be a nucleus with A \geq 2 nucleons, with each crossing between nucleons of types \tau_i and \tau_j at generator \sigma_i the linear element c\,\sigma_i + d \in H_A(q), and let

\Xi_A \;=\; \prod_{i=0}^{A-2} \; \prod_{j=A-1}^{i+1} \bigl(c_{ji}\,\sigma_i + d_{ji}\bigr)

be the block-ordered nucleus element (blocks ordered by increasing generator index; the inner product taken in decreasing j, matching the transfer-matrix order). Then the Gröbner--Shirshov reduction of \Xi_A:

  1. uses only the Hecke rule \sigma_i^2 \to (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1 — zero Yang--Baxter and zero far-commutativity steps along every reduction path, and the block computation takes at most \binom{A-1}{2} block multiplications, each one use of the Hecke relation;
  2. terminates in the chain form 
    \bar{\mathcal{N}}(A) \;=\; \prod_{i=0}^{A-2} \bigl(a_i\,\sigma_i + b_i\bigr),
    whose coefficients (a_i, b_i) are produced by the transfer-matrix recurrence \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} a_i' \\ b_i' \end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = T(c, d)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} a_i \\ b_i \end{smallmatrix}\bigr);
  3. and the full expansion \sum_{S} \bigl(\prod_{i \in S} a_i\bigr)\bigl(\prod_{i \notin S} b_i\bigr)\,\sigma_S, over subsets S \subseteq \{0, \ldots, A-2\} with \sigma_S the product of the \sigma_i, i \in S, in increasing order, is the exact Gröbner--Shirshov normal form of \Xi_A.

Here the Gröbner--Shirshov rewriting system for H_A(q) has three families of rules — the Hecke rule, far-commutativity \sigma_j\sigma_i \to \sigma_i\sigma_j for j \geq i + 2, and the Bokut--Shiao family \sigma_j\sigma_{j-1}\cdots\sigma_k\sigma_j \to \sigma_{j-1}\sigma_j\sigma_{j-1}\cdots\sigma_k for k \leq j - 1, whose case k = j - 1 is Yang--Baxter \sigma_j\sigma_i\sigma_j \to \sigma_i\sigma_j\sigma_i with j = i + 1. With Yang--Baxter in place of the whole Bokut--Shiao family the system is not confluent once A \geq 4. The completed system is a Gröbner--Shirshov basis and is confluent by the Diamond Lemma [bergman1978], so the normal form is unique and independent of the reduction order (Hecke normal form).
prf:tm-gs-normal-form:
Proof Proof of the Hecke-only Gröbner--Shirshov reduction. The proof is by induction on the nucleon count A.

Inductive claim. For every A \geq 2, the reduction of \Xi_A uses only the Hecke rule, and the result is the chain form

\bar{\mathcal{N}}(A) \;=\; \prod_{i=0}^{A-2} \bigl(a_i\,\sigma_i + b_i\bigr),

whose full expansion \sum_{S} \bigl(\prod_{i \in S} a_i\bigr)\bigl(\prod_{i \notin S} b_i\bigr)\,\sigma_S, over subsets S \subseteq \{0, \ldots, A-2\} with \sigma_S the product of the \sigma_i, i \in S, in increasing order, is already in normal form.

Base case A = 2. The word is the single factor c\,\sigma_0 + d: one linear block, no reducible subword, and the chain state is (a_0, b_0) = (c, d).

Normality of the expansion. Every monomial \sigma_S of the chain form contains each generator at most once, with indices strictly increasing left to right. Such a word contains no subword \sigma_i^2 (no repeated letter), no far-commutativity leading word \sigma_j\sigma_i with j \geq i+2 (adjacent letters are strictly increasing), and no Yang--Baxter leading word \sigma_j\sigma_i\sigma_j (that pattern repeats the letter \sigma_j). Hence every \sigma_S is a normal word, and distinct S give distinct normal words, so the expansion is the unique normal-form expression.

Inductive step A \to A+1. Adding nucleon \tau_A modifies the word in exactly two ways. At each existing block i \leq A-2, one new factor c\,\sigma_i + d with (c, d) = (c_{Ai}, d_{Ai}) enters on the left of the block. Inside that block,

\bigl(c\,\sigma_i + d\bigr)\bigl(a_i\,\sigma_i + b_i\bigr)
\;=\;
c\,a_i\,\sigma_i^2 + \bigl(c\,b_i + d\,a_i\bigr)\sigma_i + d\,b_i ,

and the single occurrence of \sigma_i^2 is the only reducible subword created: the letters adjacent to the block across its boundaries carry strictly smaller (left) and strictly larger (right) generator indices, so no far-commutativity pattern arises, and a Yang--Baxter pattern would need the same letter twice separated by one position, which the block structure never produces. One application of the Hecke rule \sigma_i^2 \to (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1 gives

a_i' \;=\; a_i c\,(q - q^{-1}) + a_i d + b_i c,
\qquad
b_i' \;=\; a_i c + b_i d,

which is precisely the transfer-matrix recurrence \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} a_i' \\ b_i' \end{smallmatrix}\bigr) = T(c, d)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} a_i \\ b_i \end{smallmatrix}\bigr). Second, one new block c\,\sigma_{A-1} + d appears at the right end of the word, already linear, requiring no reduction. The result is again a block-ordered product of linear factors, so the inductive claim holds for A+1.

Conclusion. By induction, the reduction of \Xi_A to \bar{\mathcal{N}}(A) uses Hecke reductions only: one per crossing after the first at each generator (none when the running coefficient a_i vanishes, as happens for purely scalar crossing types with c = 0), for a total of at most \binom{A}{2} - (A-1) = \binom{A-1}{2} block multiplications, each one use of the Hecke relation, and zero Yang--Baxter, far-commutativity or other Bokut--Shiao steps. The chain-form words are strictly increasing, so they contain no repeated generator and hence no leading word of the Hecke rule or of the Bokut--Shiao family, and no far-commutativity leading word. Since the completed rewriting system is confluent [bergman1978] and the chain-form expansion consists of pairwise distinct normal words, the chain is the exact Gröbner--Shirshov normal form of the nucleus element. \blacksquare
def:witness-4he:

def:witness-8be:

def:witness-12c:

  F_{\mathrm{Pauli}}^{(12)} \approx 0.129

rem:witness-computation-method:
Remark Witness computation method: inductive Gröbner--Shirshov reduction. An inductive Gröbner–Shirshov reduction is the natural vehicle for the Pauli witnesses. It runs entirely in exact Laurent arithmetic over \mathbb{Z}[\check{q}, \check{q}^{-1}], preventing floating-point error accumulation during algebraic reduction, and grows the braid one strand at a time in lockstep with the mass-number induction in H_A(q).

Crossing convention

All computations use the unimodular (1, -h_{\mathrm{A}}) crossing convention, writing h_{\mathrm{A}} = q - q^{-1} for the Hecke relation's discriminant:

Crossing type (c, d) Source
\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{p} (proton–proton) (1, 0) positive crossing \sigma
\mathfrak{n}\mathfrak{n} (neutron–neutron) (1, -h_{\mathrm{A}}) negative crossing \sigma^{-1} = \sigma - (q - q^{-1})
\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{n} (mixed) (1, -h_{\mathrm{A}}/2) averaged \tfrac{1}{2}(\sigma + \sigma^{-1})

This yields \det T_{nn} = -1 (unimodular), consistent with the Iwahori–Hecke inverse relation.

Inductive construction

The engine builds the normal form strand by strand, from A = 2 up to the target mass number. At each step A \to A + 1:

  1. Extend: multiply the current normal form by the transfer matrix entry (c \cdot \sigma_{A-1} + d), where c and d are the crossing coefficients from the table above.
  2. Reduce: apply the Iwahori–Hecke relation \sigma_i^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1 to eliminate all non-reduced words.
  3. Strip I_8 (the adjacency-correlation ideal): absorb adjacency correlations \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} into single-generator terms.
  4. Strip I_9 (the closed-shell-chain ideal): collapse closed shell chains by absorbing w \cdot \sigma_j into its prefix w when both are present.
  5. Accumulate: update the Pauli accumulator \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{alt}} = \sum_w c_w \cdot (-q^{-1})^{\ell(w)} and the net trace \mathrm{net} = \sum_w c_w \cdot q^{\ell(w)}.

Steps 3 and 4 project the expanded terms to keep the support bounded: quotienting each extended word through the adjacency and chain-collapse ideals absorbs structurally determined words back into the per-generator transfer-matrix factorization, avoiding the A! dimension growth of H_A(q).

Arithmetic

Intermediate computations use exact Laurent polynomials in \mathbb{Z}[\check{q}, \check{q}^{-1}], where \check{q} = q^{1/2} is the spinor information rate. No real-number specialization enters until final evaluation at q_0. The denominator 2^{p_n} (from the averaged \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{n} crossing) is tracked separately and cancels in the Pauli ratio F_{\mathrm{Pauli}} = |\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{alt}}| / |\mathrm{net}|.

Scalability

For A \leq 12, the symbolic Laurent polynomial reduction completes directly. For medium and heavy nuclei (A \geq 13), factored 2 \times 2 monotone transfer-matrix evaluation at q_0 is carried out in arbitrary-precision arithmetic (\ge 80 decimal digits, zero IEEE-754 binary64 rounding), avoiding exponential polynomial expansion while preserving full numerical precision.
sec:tm-worked-examples-intro: Before applying the transfer-matrix construction at scale, its mechanics are made concrete on the smallest tractable nuclei, where each evaluation can be followed step by step. The worked examples that follow carry this out for the light nuclei, from hydrogen through carbon.
tm-worked-examples:
Worked examples (light nuclei).

These examples work the complete transfer matrix computation for small nuclei by hand. The light nuclei are small enough that the abstract construction can be verified by eye. Walking through them makes the \binom{A}{2} cost concrete: one transfer-matrix multiplication per nucleon pair.

Throughout these symbolic formulas, z = q^3/(q^2+1) = q^2/[2]_q denotes the Markov trace weight (z(q_0^{(p)}) \approx 0.612688). Because both z(q) and the transfer matrices T(c, d) \in \mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac{1}{2}][q^{\pm 1}]) are rational functions of integer powers of q, every factor \hat{V}_i(q) and nuclear Skein polynomial P_{\mathcal{N}}(q) lies in \mathbb{Q}(q) with no half-integer powers q^{1/2}.

Example 1: Hydrogen (A = 1, Z = 1)

Hydrogen fixes the empty-product convention. With one proton there are no nucleon pairs, hence zero generators and zero transfer matrix multiplications.

  P_{{}^1\mathrm{H}}(q) = 1 \quad\text{(empty product)}

Hydrogen has no nuclear Skein polynomial. Its mass comes entirely from the proton's internal knot structure and the electron shell.

Example 2: Deuterium (A = 2, Z = 1, N = 1)

Deuterium is the first case with braiding: one proton and one neutron, ordered as [\mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{n}]. This single pair gives one generator \sigma_0 with one mixed \mathfrak{p}-\mathfrak{n} crossing. The transfer matrix is:

  M_0(q) = T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} & 1 \\[4pt] 1 & -\frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} \end{pmatrix}

Taking the Markov trace against z gives the traced volume:

  \hat{V}_0(q) = z \cdot (M_0)_{11} + (M_0)_{21} = z \cdot \frac{q - q^{-1}}{2} + 1

The nuclear Skein polynomial is this single factor:

  P_{{}^2\mathrm{H}}(q) = \hat{V}_0(q)

This rational function in \mathbb{Q}(q) requires \binom{2}{2} = 1 matrix evaluation.

Example 3: Helium-3 (A = 3, Z = 2, N = 1)

Helium-3 is the first case with a genuine product of transfer matrices. Its nucleons are [\mathfrak{p}_0, \mathfrak{p}_1, \mathfrak{n}_2], giving generators \sigma_0 and \sigma_1.

At generator \sigma_0, there are two crossings: (0, 1) and (0, 2). See Table 1. The product in decreasing j is:

  M_0(q) = T_{pp}(q) \cdot T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q)

The traced volume is \hat{V}_0(q) = z \cdot (M_0)_{11} + (M_0)_{21}.

At generator \sigma_1, there is one crossing: (1, 2). See Table 2.

  M_1(q) = T_{\mathrm{mix}}(q)

The traced volume is \hat{V}_1(q) = z \cdot (T_{\mathrm{mix}})_{11} + (T_{\mathrm{mix}})_{21}.

The nuclear Skein polynomial is:

  P_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}(q) = \hat{V}_0(q) \cdot \hat{V}_1(q)

This requires \binom{3}{2} = 3 multiplications.

Example 4: Helium-4 (A = 4, Z = 2, N = 2)

Helium-4 shows the full triangular pattern. Nucleons [\mathfrak{p}_0, \mathfrak{p}_1, \mathfrak{n}_2, \mathfrak{n}_3] give generators \sigma_0, \sigma_1, \sigma_2 carrying three, two, and one crossings.

  • \sigma_0 (3 crossings): M_0(q) = T_{pp} \cdot T_{\mathrm{mix}} \cdot T_{\mathrm{mix}} (See Table 3)
  • \sigma_1 (2 crossings): M_1(q) = T_{\mathrm{mix}} \cdot T_{\mathrm{mix}} (See Table 4)
  • \sigma_2 (1 crossing): M_2(q) = T_{nn} (See Table 5)

The nuclear Skein polynomial is:

  P_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}(q) = \hat{V}_0(q) \cdot \hat{V}_1(q) \cdot \hat{V}_2(q)

This requires \binom{4}{2} = 6 multiplications.

Example 5: Tritium beta decay ({}^3\mathrm{H} \to {}^3\mathrm{He})

Converting nucleon: position 1 (\mathfrak{n} \to \mathfrak{p}).

Parent ({}^3\mathrm{H}):

  • \sigma_0: M_0^{\mathrm{par}} = T_{\mathrm{mix}} \cdot T_{\mathrm{mix}} (See Table 6)
  • \sigma_1: M_1^{\mathrm{par}} = T_{nn} (See Table 7)

Daughter ({}^3\mathrm{He}):

  • \sigma_0: M_0^{\mathrm{dau}} = T_{pp} \cdot T_{\mathrm{mix}} (See Table 8)
  • \sigma_1: M_1^{\mathrm{dau}} = T_{\mathrm{mix}} (See Table 9)

Change at each generator: At \sigma_0, only (0,1) changes (T_{\mathrm{mix}} \to T_{pp}): \Delta M_0 = T_{\mathrm{mix}} \cdot \Delta_\beta. At \sigma_1, (1,2) changes (T_{nn} \to T_{\mathrm{mix}}): \Delta M_1 = \Delta_\beta.

The Q-value is:

  \ln \frac{P_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}}{P_{{}^3\mathrm{H}}} = \ln \frac{\hat{V}_0^{\mathrm{dau}}}{\hat{V}_0^{\mathrm{par}}} + \ln \frac{\hat{V}_1^{\mathrm{dau}}}{\hat{V}_1^{\mathrm{par}}}

sec:tm-heavy-atom-examples-intro: The transfer-matrix evaluation was first exercised on light nuclei, where the nucleon count is small. Heavy atoms test whether that evaluation holds as the count grows across the periodic table. The worked examples below form an increasing-mass ladder — {}^{14}\mathrm{C} \to {}^{14}\mathrm{N}, {}^{60}\mathrm{Co} \to {}^{60}\mathrm{Ni}, and {}^{210}\mathrm{Bi} \to {}^{210}\mathrm{Po} — and carry the transfer-matrix evaluation through each in turn.
tm-heavy-atom-examples:
Heavy-atom worked examples.

The light-nucleus examples use only the bare transfer matrix product. For heavy nuclei, shell corrections from the magic number structure become essential. This section works through the full Q-value algorithm. These examples demonstrate the mechanics: a definite Q-value output from the aether parameter q alone. The worked numbers below are conditional on the three shell-structure conjectures (C1)–(C3) — the magic-number set is observed, not yet derived from q; the dominant-binding-operator selection and the inner-shell cancellation are unproven. Where a residual remains, it is bracketed as an open direction under those conjectures, not absorbed into a free parameter.

Recall: s = q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}, z = q^3/(q^2+1) = q^2/[2]_q, \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}, E_{\times} = \frac{1}{2}(q - q^{-1}), and \mu_0 the conversion constant carrying the dimensionless bracket into \mathrm{MeV}. Exact 80-digit bare transfer-matrix Q-values at z(q_0^{(p)}) = q_0^{(p)3}/(q_0^{(p)2}+1) are tabulated in Table A.3; the illustrative intermediate shell numerals in Examples 6--8 below retain an earlier pre-rationalized loop normalization and serve only to display the combinatorial structure of the \binom{A}{2} generator sweep.

The magic number table

Shell closures occur at specific nucleon counts where the Gröbner--Shirshov word-length histogram is palindromic:

  \mathcal{M} = \{0, 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126\}

For nucleon count X, see Table 1. When X is magic (n_{\mathrm{out}} = 0), the outermost shell is closed and the relevant shell size is n_{\mathrm{shell}}(X).

The Q-value algorithm (summary)

Input: (Z, N), aether parameter q.

  1. Compute outer shell occupancies for parent (Z, N) and daughter (Z+1, N-1).
  2. Compute torus knot Markov traces \tau(n) for each occupancy from the Chebyshev recurrence.
  3. Compute bare Skein polynomial ratio R_{\mathrm{bare}} = \log_q(P_{\mathrm{dau}} / P_{\mathrm{par}}).
  4. Compute shell correction \Delta_{\mathrm{shell}} = (\text{proton shell change}) + (\text{neutron shell change}).
  5. Add weak vertex \Delta_{T_{3,5}} = -3.370.
  6. Convert: Q = |R_{\mathrm{bare}} + \Delta_{\mathrm{shell}} + \Delta_{T_{3,5}}| \times \hbar_q \cdot E_{\times} \cdot \mu_0.

Example 6: Carbon-14 (A = 14, Z = 6, N = 8)

{}^{14}\mathrm{C} \to {}^{14}\mathrm{N} (\beta^-: \mathfrak{d} \to \mathfrak{u} at one neutron).

This is the anomalously slow decay (t_{1/2} = 5730 yr, \log ft = 9.04). The shell structure explains why.

See Table 2. The parent has a closed neutron shell at n = 8. The daughter breaks it (N = 8 \to N' = 7).

Parent {}^{14}\mathrm{C}(6, 8): 13 generators, \binom{14}{2} = 91 matrix multiplications. Nucleon ordering: [\underbrace{\mathfrak{p} \cdots \mathfrak{p}}_{6} \underbrace{\mathfrak{n} \cdots \mathfrak{n}}_{8}]. The converting neutron (position 6) affects \sigma_0 through \sigma_6.

See Table 3. Generator \sigma_6 carries nearly half the total energy change (-1.660 of -3.361). Its chiral degree k_6 = 7 means all 7 crossings with downstream nucleons change type.
